approachQuestion.prompt:
A distant log entry

A read-only interface get(i) accepts any nonnegative integer index and returns either the integer at index i or END when i is outside a hidden finite length n. Valid entries are strictly increasing. END compares greater than every integer. Given target x, return its index or -1. 0 <= n <= 10^9. Each get costs one probe. Examples: hidden [4,9,15,22], x=15 -> 2; hidden [], x=1 -> -1. Minimize worst-case probes in terms of where x would be inserted.
constraints: Use only the stated input ordering and access guarantees.

options.text: Probe index 0, then 1,2,4,... until a value >=x or END brackets the insertion position. Iteratively binary-search the resulting index interval and verify equality.
options.feedback: Doubling creates a finite bracket without knowing the length; ordered probes then locate the insertion point.

options.text: Cache every get result in a balanced dictionary while running the same bracketing and search.
options.feedback: It is correct, but storing every probe is unnecessary: scalar bounds suffice for this interface.

options.text: Stop and return -1 as soon as a probed valid value is not equal to x.
options.feedback: For hidden [4,9,15,22], x=15, index 0 is unequal although target exists at index 2.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For target-method, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. p is the lower-bound insertion index of x, between 0 and n. Count interface probes as time; arithmetic and END tests are constant time. Indices cannot overflow, and only scalar bounds are retained. Input storage and returned result storage are excluded; all temporary buffers and call stacks are included.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Count all working memory including any stack; exclude supplied inputs and the scalar result.

feedback.reason: Doubling and subsequent halving each require logarithmically many probes in p+1.
details: Doubling reaches a bracket around insertion index p after O(log(p+2)) probes. The bracket width is proportional to p+1, so binary search needs the same order of probes. Add these phases; retain only scalar bracket indices and probe results.
“O(log(p + 2)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Doubling creates a finite bracket without knowing the length; ordered probes then locate the insertion point.
“O(n*n + 1) time, O(n + 1) auxiliary space”: Doubling brackets the insertion position and binary search halves that bracket; no full-array or pairwise scan or n-entry index is built.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Insertion positions can grow arbitrarily far from zero, requiring additional doubling probes before search.
